The person behind the technology

An AI and technology enthusiast with a scientist’s training and an educator’s daily practice.

I am Fahad, an AI and technology enthusiast interested in exploring intelligent systems, solving complex technical problems, and understanding how emerging technologies can create meaningful real-world impact.

My interests span artificial intelligence, software problem-solving, data analysis, intelligent automation, LLM applications, and scientific research. I learn by building and testing: working daily with AI tools for research, drafting, data tasks and teaching material, and studying how agentic workflows, retrieval systems and automation platforms are actually put together.

My long-term vision is to make artificial intelligence accessible, understandable, and beneficial for the next generation — particularly through responsible AI-powered primary education, where technology supports teachers and children’s own thinking rather than replacing either.

My scientific background is a BS in Biochemistry from Abdul Wali Khan University Mardan (AWKUM) — molecular biology, metabolism, enzymology and laboratory methods — which shaped how I approach every problem: ask precise questions, test ideas, and let evidence settle arguments. My final-year research, a hospital-based dengue study, is presented in full in the Research section.

Professionally, I serve as a Primary School Teacher (PST) with the Elementary & Secondary Education Department (ESED), Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, at Government Primary School Koz Kalay, Buner, since October 2022 — where I am also the school’s focal person for digital data work: student profiles, results uploading and EMIS returns. Before government service, I taught for a year at Fuji Public School, Khanano Dherai.

AI & Technology

Artificial Intelligence — the field as a whole

The umbrella discipline, and how its branches relate to each other.

+

What it is

Artificial intelligence is the field of building systems that perform tasks associated with human intelligence — recognising patterns, understanding language, generating content, making decisions. It is an umbrella, not a single technology.

How the branches relate

Machine learning is the main modern approach: systems learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules. Deep learning is machine learning with large multi-layer neural networks. From deep learning grow the specialities: natural language processing (language), computer vision (images), generative AI (creating content), multimodal AI (combining text, image and audio), and AI agents (systems that plan and use tools). Large language models sit at the centre of most current progress because one deep-learning architecture — the transformer — turned out to work across all of these.

Problems it addresses

Searching and summarising information, translation, pattern detection in data too large for humans, accessibility (speech-to-text, text-to-speech), drafting and creative assistance, and automation of routine cognitive work.

Limitations

AI systems do not understand the world as humans do; they reproduce patterns from training data. They can be confidently wrong, inherit bias from data, and fail outside the situations they were trained on. Capability is not comprehension — see the comparison table in the Laboratory.

My level: area of active exploration

AI-Assisted Data Analysis

A disciplined process, with AI helping — never replacing the checking.

+

The process

Collection→Cleaning→Missing values→Transformation→Exploration→Statistics→Visualisation→Interpretation→Reporting→Quality checking

Data analysis starts long before any chart: collecting the right data, cleaning errors and duplicates, deciding honestly how to handle missing values, and reshaping data into analysable form. Exploration and statistics come next; visualisation makes patterns visible; interpretation asks what the patterns actually mean — and quality checking asks whether any of it can be trusted.

Tools

Python with Pandas (tables and cleaning), NumPy (numerical computation) and Matplotlib (charts), plus classical statistical methods. AI assistants help write and debug code, suggest checks and draft explanations of results.

Limitations

AI can produce plausible-looking analysis of bad data. A model cannot know that a column was recorded wrongly or that a sample is unrepresentative — the analyst must. Findings from a biased or tiny dataset stay unreliable no matter how polished the chart.

My level: practical experience — school data, results and research data

Python & Scientific Computing

The working language of data, science and AI.

+

What it is

Python is a readable, general-purpose programming language that became the default tool of scientific computing and AI because of its ecosystem: NumPy for arrays and mathematics, Pandas for data, Matplotlib for plots, and the major machine-learning libraries.

What it is used for

Data processing and cleaning, scientific calculation, statistical analysis, automation of repetitive file and data tasks, calling APIs to connect services, building small tools, and developing and evaluating AI models.

Problems it addresses

Work that is too large, too repetitive or too error-prone by hand — thousands of records checked in seconds, the same calculation applied consistently, results that can be re-run and verified.

Limitations

Python is slower than compiled languages for raw computation (libraries work around this), and code is only as correct as the person who checks it. An AI assistant can draft code quickly; running, testing and understanding it remains the human’s job.

My level: hands-on familiarity, still developing

No-Code Automation & Workflow Integration

Connecting services so routine work flows by itself — with a human in control.

+

How it works

Automation platforms connect applications through triggers (something happens), conditions (checks along the way) and actions (do this next). Services communicate through APIs — defined ways for software to talk to software — and webhooks, which let one service notify another the moment an event occurs. Platforms such as n8n, Make and Zapier provide these connections visually, without writing a full program.

A conceptual workflow

Form submission→Validation→AI processing→Human approval→Report→Notification

This workflow is conceptual — shown to explain the pattern, not connected to any live service from this page. Note the approval step: well-designed automation pauses for a human before anything consequential happens.

Problems it addresses

Copying data between systems, routine notifications, report assembly, and follow-ups that humans forget — freeing attention for work that needs judgement.

Limitations

Automations break silently when a connected service changes; errors propagate at machine speed; and every connection is a place personal data can leak. Monitoring and error handling are part of the design, not extras.

My level: hands-on familiarity

AI Governance & Quality Control

Why AI output must be evaluated before it is trusted.

+

What it covers

Governance is the discipline of using AI responsibly: testing systems against evaluation datasets before deployment, measuring accuracy and reliability, watching for bias, protecting privacy, being transparent about limitations, and keeping human oversight over consequential decisions.

The central failure: hallucination

Language models generate text that sounds right; when the pattern runs out, they may invent facts, references or figures with complete confidence. Quality control therefore means source-checking important claims, testing on known-answer cases, and designing systems that can say “I don’t know.”

Problems it addresses

Preventing wrong, unfair or unsafe AI output from reaching people who trust it — in classrooms, offices and public services alike.

Limitations

Evaluation can only test what someone thought to test. Governance reduces risk; it does not certify perfection, and it must continue after deployment, not stop at launch.

My level: practical concern — applied daily in checking AI-assisted work

LLM Application Development

How applications are built on top of large language models.

+

The building blocks

Models read text as tokens — small chunks of words (try the tokenizer in the Laboratory). Each token becomes an embedding, a list of numbers capturing meaning, and the model can only consider a limited amount of text at once: its context window. Prompt engineering and system instructions shape behaviour within that window.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

RAG connects a model to real documents: the question is embedded, a vector database finds the most similar stored passages by number-distance, and those passages are placed in the context so the answer can be grounded in them. It is how chatbots answer from a specific handbook or record set.

Problems it addresses

Assistants that answer from an organisation’s own material, document question-answering, summarisation and drafting tools grounded in supplied sources.

Limitations — honestly

Retrieval does not guarantee correctness. The search can fetch the wrong passage, the right passage can be misread, and the model can still add unsupported claims. RAG grounds answers; it does not certify them. Output evaluation remains essential.

My level: area of exploration

AI Agentic Workflows

From answering questions to carrying out multi-step tasks — under permission.

+

The loop

Goal→Planning→Tool selection→Execution→Evaluation→Response

An agent differs from a chatbot: given a goal, it breaks the task into steps, chooses tools (search, files, code, other services), executes, observes the result, corrects course, and reports back. Memory lets it use context across steps.

Why permissions matter

An agent that can act can also act wrongly — at speed. Safe design means limited tool permissions, clear boundaries, logging, and human approval before irreversible or sensitive steps. The Laboratory’s agent explorer shows exactly where that approval gate belongs.

Problems it addresses

Multi-step research, document processing, data tasks and productivity workflows that are too long for a single prompt but too judgement-light to need a human at every keystroke.

Limitations

Errors compound across steps; a wrong early assumption can steer a whole run. Agents need evaluation at each stage, not only at the end — and a human who actually reads the report.

My level: hands-on familiarity — daily work with an AI assistant

Generative AI

Systems that create — text, images, audio, video — and the responsibilities that come with them.

+

The forms

Text generation, image generation and editing, video and image-to-video, speech and audio generation, multimodal creation that mixes them, AI-assisted website creation, and creative automation — producing variations, drafts and material at a speed no manual workflow matches.

Problems it addresses

Drafting, visual material for teaching where no photographer exists, prototyping ideas before investing in them, and accessibility formats (the same content as text, speech or image).

Risks

The same power creates misinformation at scale, copyright questions about training material and outputs, and identity misuse — synthetic images or voices of real people. Generated content should be labelled as generated, and never used to impersonate.

Limitations

Generative models optimise for plausibility, not truth or originality. Output quality varies, styles converge toward the average of training data, and human editing remains the difference between raw generation and good work.

My level: practical experience — image creation, editing and AI-assisted websites

Software Engineering & Technical Problem-Solving

The craft underneath everything above.

+

The principles

Architecture (how a system is divided into parts), debugging (finding why behaviour differs from intention), API integration (connecting systems through defined interfaces), testing (proving behaviour before users depend on it), and performance and security analysis — understanding how software behaves, breaks, and can be misused, so it can be built defensively.

Problems it addresses

Everything from a school data workflow that keeps failing, to a phone fault diagnosed step by step: isolate the variable, reproduce the problem, test one change at a time, verify the fix.

A boundary, stated plainly

Security analysis and understanding systems belong to legitimate, authorised work only — one’s own systems, or systems one is permitted to test. Understanding how something works is a skill; bypassing other people’s access controls is not a service offered here.

Limitations

Problem-solving is bounded by access, documentation and honesty about uncertainty: a verified procedure is worth more than a confident guess, and reversible diagnostics come before risky ones.

My level: practical experience — devices, systems and school technology

Touch how intelligence works

Every exhibit here genuinely runs in your browser. Scenes load only when you reach them, pause off-screen, and each one is labelled for what it is — a simplified educational model, never a claim about a real commercial system.

3D Neural Network Explorer

A simplified conceptual model: an input layer, two hidden layers and an output layer. Drag to rotate, scroll or pinch to zoom, click any neuron to inspect it, and send a signal to watch activation travel through the connections. Real networks have millions to billions of neurons; the principle — weighted connections, activations passed forward — is the same.

Network idle — 4 inputs · 6 + 5 hidden · 3 outputs

How a neural network works

Each neuron receives numbers from the previous layer, multiplies them by learned weights, adds them up, and passes the result through an activation function that decides how strongly it “fires”. Training means adjusting millions of such weights, a little at a time, so the outputs get less wrong. Click a neuron to inspect its role.

Text alternative: information enters at the input layer as numbers, is combined and transformed by two hidden layers, and leaves the output layer as a prediction. Learning = adjusting connection weights from examples.

Language models do not read words; they read tokens — chunks of text converted to numbers. Computer Vision — how machines “see”

Conceptual simulation, labelled as such — no real vision model runs on this page. A real system turns an image into pixels, extracts features (edges, shapes, textures), then classifies or detects objects and reports a confidence score — a probability, not certainty. Press the button to see the shape of that process:

Limitations of real systems: they fail on unusual angles, poor light, and images unlike their training data — and a 92% confidence score still means roughly 8 in 100 such calls are wrong.

Human Intelligence vs Artificial Intelligence

An honest comparison. Current AI systems are not conscious, do not have experiences, feelings or understanding in the human sense — they process patterns. That difference is not a flaw to hide; it is the fact the whole comparison turns on.

DimensionHuman intelligenceArtificial intelligence
LearningLearns from few examples, through experience, emotion and social context; transfers learning between unrelated areas.Learns statistical patterns from very large datasets; transfers narrowly and can fail outside its training distribution.
ReasoningUses common sense, causality and lived knowledge of how the physical and social world works.Produces reasoning-shaped output from patterns; can be fluent and still wrong about simple cause and effect.
CreativityCreates from intention, experience and meaning; knows why a work matters.Recombines patterns from training data into novel outputs; has no intention or stake in the result.
MemorySelective, reconstructive, tied to emotion and identity; forgets — which is often useful.Precise within its context window and stored data; remembers nothing between sessions unless a system is built to store it.
UnderstandingGenuine comprehension grounded in a body, a life and a world.No verified understanding or consciousness; competence at tasks must not be mistaken for awareness.
ResponsibilityHumans are accountable for their decisions and can be answerable for harm.An AI system cannot be responsible. Responsibility always rests with the humans who build, deploy and use it.

AI for the Next Generation

Preparing Young Minds for an Intelligent Future.

My long-term ambition: explore how artificial intelligence can make primary education more understandable, interactive, personalised and accessible — never to replace teachers or human relationships, always to support better learning.

AI-Assisted Primary Learning

Patient, level-aware support across the primary curriculum:

  • Mathematics — concepts built step by step, with visual examples
  • English & reading — stories, comprehension questions, gentle correction
  • Vocabulary — new words introduced in context, then practised
  • Science — big ideas explained with everyday examples
  • Creative thinking & problem-solving — prompts that open thinking rather than closing it with an answer

AI Literacy for Children

Children who will grow up with AI deserve honest answers early:

  • What is AI? — a tool that learns patterns, not a person
  • Can AI make mistakes? — yes, confidently; that is why we check
  • Why question answers? — checking is a strength, not rudeness
  • Humans vs AI — feelings, responsibility and understanding are human
  • Protect personal information — never share names, photos or secrets with any app

The Human Role

AI should strengthen human intelligence, not replace independent thinking. Teachers and parents remain essential — for judgement, encouragement, values, safety and love of learning. The technology’s place is beside the teacher: preparing material, offering practice, and freeing time for the human work only humans do.

Principle: AI supports · humans teach

Personalised Learning, Step by Step

How a good educational assistant responds when a child is stuck on multiplication — support for understanding, not a shortcut past it:

Recognise the difficulty

The child answers 6 × 7 incorrectly twice. The assistant notices the pattern instead of just marking it wrong.

Explain simply

“6 × 7 means six groups of seven — like six bags with seven marbles in each.”

Show a visual example

Six rows of seven dots appear; the child counts along the rows.

Give a guided exercise

“Now you try: what is 6 × 5? Use the rows if you need them.”

Offer a hint, not the answer

If the child stalls: “You know 6 × 5 is five sixes… count by sixes: 6, 12, 18…”

Check understanding

“Well done. Can you tell me in your own words what 6 × 7 means?”

Another example if needed

Understanding confirmed — or another example, patiently, until it is.

Children’s Privacy & Safety Principles

  • Age-appropriate content, with parent and teacher supervision
  • Minimal data — a learning tool needs almost no personal information about a child
  • No profiling of children, no advertising, no engagement tricks
  • Clear boundaries: the assistant teaches; it is not a friend, and says so
  • Human oversight of anything a child-facing system produces
  • On this page: no data is collected from children — or from anyone

Research, presented honestly

One real study, presented in full with its numbers exactly as recorded and its status stated without decoration — plus the research directions I am growing toward.

Featured study · Original research manuscript

Demographic, clinical and serological profile of dengue patients admitted to Mardan Medical Complex, Pakistan, October 2019 – January 2020

Shah Fahad · Muhammad Ayaz Khan
Department of Biochemistry, Faculty of Chemical and Life Sciences, Abdul Wali Khan University Mardan, Pakistan · Supervisor: Dr. Sulaiman, Associate Professor
Hospital-based descriptive survey n = 153 admitted patients Oct 2019 – Jan 2020 Manuscript — not published or peer-reviewed
153laboratory-confirmed patients included
72.5%male — 111 men, 42 women
53%of cases admitted in October, the peak month
≈44%knew mosquitoes transmit dengue (68 of 153)

Background. Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral disease spread by Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus. Hospital-based data from district Mardan are scarce.

Methods. Admitted, laboratory-confirmed dengue patients at Mardan Medical Complex were interviewed face to face with a 23-item questionnaire between October 2019 and January 2020. Infection was confirmed by immunochromatographic test (ICT) for NS1 antigen, IgG and IgM. Data were analysed descriptively in Microsoft Excel.

Findings. Of 153 patients, 111 were men (72.5%) and 42 women (27.5%). Most were aged 15–30 years (n=63) or 45–70 years (n=44). Unemployed people (34%) and labourers (25%) predominated, and 69.9% were married. Cases peaked in October (53%). All patients had fever and headache, and all were NS1 positive; 86 were also IgG positive, 29 IgM positive and 38 positive for both. About 44% knew that mosquito bites transmit dengue.

Interpretation. Admitted dengue patients were mainly young and middle-aged men, with a clear post-monsoon peak and low awareness of transmission. Education and vector control should start before autumn. Because this was a hospital-based sample of admitted patients, these findings describe who reached this hospital — they cannot be used to calculate population prevalence or incidence.

Keywords: dengue; Mardan; Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; NS1; IgG; IgM; awareness

Integrity

What this study can — and cannot — claim

A single-centre, hospital-based study of admitted patients over four months. It has no population denominator, so incidence and prevalence cannot be calculated; severity grading, platelet counts and serotypes were not reported; and no inferential statistics were used. Methods in brief: face-to-face interviews with a 23-item questionnaire; ICT for NS1, IgG and IgM; descriptive analysis in Microsoft Excel. Discussion in brief: the October peak matches post-monsoon mosquito activity; the male predominance may reflect outdoor exposure or unequal access to hospital care, and cannot prove dengue is truly more frequent in men; the awareness gap — only ≈44% knew the mosquito route — argues for education campaigns before autumn, removal of standing water, and early consultation for fever during outbreaks. Declarations: ethics approval details, funding and conflicts of interest are not stated in the paper — details to be confirmed by the author. References in the manuscript: Gubler DJ, Clinical Microbiology Reviews 1998; WHO, Dengue haemorrhagic fever: diagnosis, treatment, prevention and control, 2nd ed., 1997.

Storage: your information is stored with Google Firebase. Your password is held only by Firebase Authentication in hashed form — it is never stored in plain text and never visible to the site owner.

Deletion: you can ask for your account and data to be deleted at any time by emailing fahadkz155@gmail.com.
